item.title: Working for Foreign Clients from Tashkent
item.summary: A developer in Tashkent explains what it really takes to work for clients abroad: time zones, contracts, payments and trust.
item.content_markdown:
When Jasur tells people that he works for a company in Berlin, they usually imagine an office with a view of the river. In fact, his office is a desk by the window of his flat in Chilonzor, and his commute is the ten steps from the kitchen. He is one of a growing number of developers in Uzbekistan who have found clients abroad without ever leaving home.

The work itself is not so different from a local job. He writes code, joins video calls and argues politely about deadlines. What is different is everything around the work.

## Living in two time zones

The first challenge is time. Berlin is several hours behind Tashkent, so Jasur's working day starts late and finishes late. "At first I tried to be available all the time," he says. "After a month I was exhausted." Now he agrees a fixed window of shared hours with his team, and outside that window he works on tasks that do not need anyone else. Clients, he has learned, respect clear boundaries more than constant availability.

## Reading the contract

The second challenge is paperwork. A contract with a foreign client should say exactly what will be delivered, how changes are handled and when payment is due. "My first contract was one paragraph long," Jasur admits. "When the client changed the project twice, I had nothing to point to." These days he refuses to start until the scope has been written down, even for small jobs.

## Getting paid

Payments can also be complicated. Depending on the client, money may arrive through an international transfer, a freelance platform or a payment service, and each option has its own fees and delays. Jasur keeps a simple spreadsheet of every invoice and checks it every Friday. He also sets aside part of each payment for taxes, because he has seen friends get into trouble by spending everything they earned.

## Building trust from far away

Perhaps the biggest challenge is trust. A client who has never met you needs reasons to believe you will deliver. For Jasur, the answer is communication: short written updates at the end of each day, honest warnings when something is going to be late, and good English in every message. "People forgive a delay," he says. "They don't forgive silence."

Working from Tashkent for a team in another country is not a dream job without problems. But for developers who are organised and willing to learn, it can open doors that once seemed very far away.
